tEn: Proven, Better, New: Mark Pincus on Control and Betting on Yourself
tZh: 验证、优化、创新：马克·平卡斯谈掌控与押注自己
sEn: Mark Pincus, founder of Zynga, shares how childhood trauma shaped his founder mindset and his framework of proven, better, new.
sZh: Zynga 创始人马克·平卡斯分享童年创伤如何塑造他的创始人思维，以及他“验证、优化、创新”的框架。

consensus.en: Founders are often born from childhood trauma, which becomes a source of strength.
consensus.zh: 创始人往往源于童年创伤，而这会成为力量的源泉。

consensus.en: Winning instincts are greater than ideas; assume your idea is wrong 75% of the time.
consensus.zh: 制胜直觉比想法更重要；假设你的想法有75%的概率是错的。

consensus.en: Use the proven, better, new framework to deconstruct and improve existing products.
consensus.zh: 使用‘验证、改进、创新’框架来解构并改进现有产品。

consensus.en: Test more ideas in a week than your industry tests in a year to learn faster.
consensus.zh: 每周测试的想法要比行业一年测试的还多，以更快学习。

consensus.en: Micromanage until you can't be in the room; then build systems for good decisions.
consensus.zh: 微管理直到你无法在场；然后建立系统以做出正确决策。

consensus.en: Commitment requires sacrifice, and that sacrifice leads to true contentment.
consensus.zh: 承诺需要牺牲，而牺牲带来真正的满足。

contrarian.en: Don't wait for a lightning bolt idea; ideas are accessible to all, execution matters.
contrarian.zh: 不要等待灵光一现的想法；想法对所有人都可及，执行才重要。

contrarian.en: Scale is not the magic word; be in the details and micromanage early on.
contrarian.zh: 规模不是魔法词；早期要深入细节并微管理。

contrarian.en: Founders should keep control and make unpopular decisions, even against investors.
contrarian.zh: 创始人应保持控制权并做出不受欢迎的决定，即使与投资者相左。

contrarian.en: All new ideas fail at first; only combine proven elements with minimal innovation.
contrarian.zh: 所有新想法起初都会失败；只将验证过的元素与最小创新结合。

contrarian.en: The abyss between successes is normal; pursue curiosities, not just A+ ideas.
contrarian.zh: 成功之间的深渊是正常的；追求好奇心，而不仅仅是A+想法。

contrarian.en: We have latent depression because we underuse the creative power of devices.
contrarian.zh: 我们有一种潜在的抑郁，因为我们未充分利用设备的创造力。

turns.en: I had a very wonderful but strong father. You haven't become the man that I hoped you would. I said goodbye. So many founders are born out of the childhood difficulties and trauma. I've always been an outsider. These things that are remarkably painful can be the great sources of strength because at an early age you learn what you're capable of. We know there's so much power in our hands and we do so little with it. This is the founder mindset with Raza Sachu.
turns.zh: 我有一个非常出色但强势的父亲。你没有成为我希望你成为的那种人。我说了再见。很多创始人都是源于童年的困难和创伤。我一直是个局外人。这些极其痛苦的事情可以成为巨大的力量来源，因为你在很小的时候就了解了自己的能力。我们知道我们手中有如此大的力量，却很少去运用它。这是 Raza Sachu 的《创始人思维》。

turns.en: The founder mindset is not just about starting a business. It's a way of living. At its core, what it enables a person to do is to do the thing that every human being wants to have a positive impact on the people that they care about. In this podcast, what we are going to do is meet with some of the greatest founders, some of the people that have had the most improbable journeys who have lived with the founder mindset. What does it take to be a founder? Mark Pincus doesn't believe in the lightning bolt, the one brilliant idea that changes everything. He built Zingga, the social gaming giant behind Farmville and Words with Friends, and sold it for $122.7 billion. Before that, he had already built three companies. One sold, one went public, and one failed. He turned it all into a framework, proven better, new, and a habit most founders resist. Assume your idea is wrong and test it faster than anyone else. Mark Pincus, welcome to the founder mindset.
turns.zh: 创始人思维不仅仅是创业。它是一种生活方式。其核心是，它能让一个人去做每个人都想做的事情：对他们关心的人产生积极影响。在这个播客中，我们将与一些最伟大的创始人见面，一些经历过最不可思议旅程的人，他们一直践行着创始人思维。要成为一名创始人需要什么？Mark Pincus 不相信闪电般的灵感，即一个改变一切的绝妙想法。他创立了 Zingga，这是 Farmville 和 Words with Friends 背后的社交游戏巨头，并以 1227 亿美元的价格出售。在此之前，他已经创立了三家公司。一家被出售，一家上市，一家失败。他把这一切转化为一个框架，被证明更好、更新，以及大多数创始人抗拒的习惯。假设你的想法是错的，并比任何人都更快地测试它。Mark Pincus，欢迎来到《创始人思维》。

turns.en: I'm the furthest thing from an MBA that you've met.
turns.zh: 我是你见过的最不像 MBA 的人。

turns.en: No, no. I said because the future is everything this guy George Gilder wrote in this book Microcosm and you are the supertanker. You know, there wasn't internet yet and they were having dinner with him that night.
turns.zh: 不，不。我说，因为未来就是乔治·吉尔德在这本《微观宇宙》里写的一切，而你们是超级油轮。你知道，那时还没有互联网，他们那天晚上要和他共进晚餐。

turns.en: Oh, you nailed it enough that they gave me a job but then I had these career-limiting meetings with John Malone where —
turns.zh: 哦，你说得太准了，他们给了我一份工作，但后来我和约翰·马龙开了些限制职业生涯的会议，在那里——

turns.en: There was a deal that my boss or John wanted us to look at. One of them was buying a third of Prodigy, which you might remember. But it was the biggest online service, bigger than AOL. And it was 400 million for a third of the company. And I said, "This is a really dumb deal. Let me tell you why." And there's this company, AOL, that just went public and they're only worth 110 million. So we could buy the whole company and they're way better.
turns.zh: 有一个交易，我的老板或约翰想让我们看看。其中一个是收购 Prodigy 三分之一股份，你可能记得。但它是最大的在线服务，比 AOL 还大。收购三分之一要 4 亿美元。我说：“这真是个愚蠢的交易。让我告诉你为什么。”有一家公司，AOL，刚刚上市，他们只值 1.1 亿美元。所以我们可以买下整个公司，而且他们好得多。

turns.en: Where is — I mean, it's interesting, right? Because it strikes me that, and maybe you got this from your dad, but this conviction. Like, let's take the AOL story, okay? Which I mean it's a shame they didn't listen to you, but where did the conviction come from for a young person like you to feel like you could see things that others can't see?
turns.zh: 哪里——我是说，这很有趣，对吧？因为我觉得，也许你从你父亲那里继承了这种信念。比如，我们拿 AOL 的故事来说，好吧？我是说，他们没听你的真是可惜，但像你这样的年轻人，那种觉得自己能看到别人看不到的东西的信念是从哪里来的？

turns.en: That's such a good question and I call it the expert witness syndrome. So I don't think this was unique to me. I think so many people, smart people in these jobs are expert witnesses where you're closest to the data and you're closest to the answer, but you're furthest from the decision-maker. And so somebody — if John Malone, I believe, had spent the time and looked at the level of detail that I had, he would have come to the same conclusion, but he's running a big company and he was relying on other people.
turns.zh: 这个问题问得真好，我称之为专家证人综合征。所以我不认为这是我独有的。我认为很多人，这些职位上的聪明人，都是专家证人，你离数据最近，离答案最近，但离决策者最远。所以有人——我相信如果约翰·马龙花时间看了我看到的细节，他会得出同样的结论，但他在经营一家大公司，他依赖其他人。

turns.en: My proposition to you and I think I want to dive into this — instincts are greater than ideas — is effectively my proposition is what's happening is you're able to actually make decisions with uncertain information. Okay. You're actually able to look at information that's changing, that's volatile, that's not completely certain, and start trusting your judgment or instincts around it.
turns.zh: 我对你的主张，我想深入探讨一下——直觉大于想法——实际上我的主张是，正在发生的是你能够用不确定的信息做出决策。好吧。你实际上能够看着那些变化的、波动的、不完全确定的信息，并开始信任你对此的判断或直觉。

turns.en: Yes. So instinct is better than — yes — focusing on your ideas.
turns.zh: 是的。所以直觉比——是的——专注于你的想法更好。

turns.en: But first of all, I have this theory that's core to my book: we have these winning instincts that we feel in our gut. You're like, yes, I know everyone would rather order a taxi through their phone.
turns.zh: 但首先，我有个理论，是我书的核心：我们有一些赢家直觉，能在直觉中感受到。你会觉得，是的，我知道每个人都更愿意用手机叫出租车。

turns.en: But that's not something that you're getting necessarily from primary data.
turns.zh: 但那不是你一定从原始数据中得到的。

turns.en: No, that's it's lots and lots of data points that make up your life, but we have these winning instincts and then we combine them with these losing ideas that we package them in.
turns.zh: 不，那是生活中无数数据点积累的，但我们有这些赢家直觉，然后我们把它们和那些输家想法包装在一起。

turns.en: So, let's talk about—I mean, at the core, so many founders are trying to build a product and they dream about making it, taking it to mass market. Now, you have done this repeatedly, culminating in selling—you're founder of Zynga, sold it for $12.5 billion. But what's even—I mean, to me that is incredibly impressive, but what's even more impressive is it's been a repeated game for you many times. You've built these products that have broken through in a very viral way throughout the mass market. Okay. So if you were to give us—and I absolutely want to talk about your book—where I think everyone watching this podcast who's interested in building a mass market product as quickly and as efficiently as possible should read this book. Give us a thumbnail sketch of what the core principles are, your learnings around bringing a product quickly, efficiently to mass market.
turns.zh: 所以，我们来谈谈——我的意思是，本质上，很多创始人都在尝试打造产品，梦想着把它推向大众市场。现在，你已经反复做到了这一点，最终以 125 亿美元卖掉了你的公司 Zynga。但更令人印象深刻的是，这对你来说是一场重复的游戏，很多次了。你打造了这些产品，以非常病毒式的方式突破，席卷大众市场。好的。所以如果你要给我们——我绝对想谈谈你的书——我认为每个观看这个播客、有兴趣尽快高效地打造大众市场产品的人都应该读读这本书。给我们一个核心原则的简要概述，你关于快速高效地将产品推向大众市场的学习心得。

turns.en: Sure. I'd say number one, know what your goal is. Like know what—don't lose sight. I say know your goal or suffer death by a thousand compromises. So first, do you have a north star or is it I just want a product that gets traction?
turns.zh: 当然。我会说第一，知道你的目标是什么。就像知道——不要迷失方向。我说知道你的目标，否则会死于千次妥协。所以首先，你有北极星吗，还是只是想要一个能获得 traction 的产品？

turns.en: Give me an example of your north star. Like just so it's relatable. When you were starting Zynga, what was the north star?
turns.zh: 给我一个你北极星的例子。就像让它 relatable。当你创办 Zynga 时，北极星是什么？

turns.en: It was social gaming. It was eventually wrote down a mission, connect the world through games. It was improving people's relationships. We said success for us is that people moved buckets. They—that this became a new dimension in how they're doing social networking and that you and I only know each other online, but because of something I did for you in a game, you see me across the street and you cross the street to say hi. We measured number of marriages that came from our games. So, that was our north star. And so the importance of that and eventually Zynga lost sight of that and became just a game company and then it's mediocre and it's indistinguishable because that was what was special. It wasn't the entirety of it, you know, but that that was a north star. So number one, know your goal.
turns.zh: 是社交游戏。最终写下了使命：通过游戏连接世界。是改善人们的关系。我们说成功就是人们移动了桶。他们——这成为他们进行社交网络的新维度，你和我只在网上认识，但因为我为你做了游戏中的某事，你在街对面看到我，你过街来打招呼。我们衡量了来自我们游戏的婚姻数量。所以，那是我们的北极星。所以它的重要性，最终 Zynga 失去了它，变成了只是游戏公司，然后就平庸了，无法区分，因为那才是特别的。不是全部，你知道，但那是北极星。所以第一，知道你的目标。

turns.en: Number two is this fundamental principle that I really—the whole course I created at Stanford—I really want your listeners to internalize. We're a Stanford class. That's cool.
turns.zh: 第二是这个基本原则，我真的——我在斯坦福创建了整个课程——我真的希望你的听众能内化。我们是斯坦福课程。那很酷。

turns.en: It's a community college that's on the west coast. It's a feeder.
turns.zh: 那是西海岸的一所社区大学。是个 feeder。

turns.en: So the whole point of this is that we have winning instincts and they—you and I have talked about this—but they get better and better as you calibrate and you get feedback loops. Oh, I was right. It was bigger than I even thought. But we get better better two ways. The way you're saying, but it also gets better and better because we're in the arena making these decisions, building this judgment muscle.
turns.zh: 所以整个重点是，我们有赢家直觉，它们——你和我谈过这个——但随着你校准和获得反馈循环，它们会越来越好。哦，我对了。它比我以为的还要大。但我们通过两种方式变得更好。你说的方式，但也越来越好，因为我们在竞技场中做这些决定，建立这种判断力肌肉。

turns.en: Yeah. We're calibrating recalibrating along the way.
turns.zh: 是的。我们一路校准、重新校准。

turns.en: And so, so we're building these. So, we have a—there's some instinct that you feel that you're just like, like I have an instinct that everybody is lonely on some level and everybody wants to improve the relationships in their life. Okay, that seems like I'm stating the obvious.
turns.zh: 所以，我们正在建立这些。所以，我们有一个——有些直觉你感受到，就像，我有一个直觉，每个人在某种程度上都孤独，每个人都想改善生活中的关系。好吧，这似乎是我在陈述显而易见的事。

turns.en: That's great. When it's something that's everyone's agrees with, they're like, "Yeah, yeah, okay, that's a really good instinct."
turns.zh: 那很好。当它是每个人都同意的事时，他们会说，“是的，是的，好吧，那是个很好的直觉。”

turns.en: Um but then we have ideas. Just because your instinct is right does not mean that this one idea variant is going to be right. In fact, I say you can assume that your idea is right 25% of the time at best. Um even if your instinct is always right.
turns.zh: 但然后我们有想法。仅仅因为你的直觉是对的，并不意味着这个想法变体就会对。事实上，我说你可以假设你的想法最多 25% 的时候是对的。即使你的直觉总是对的。

turns.en: So then I like to say, okay, what do I do with that information? If I could go back to Mark in 2003 doing Tribe, one of the first three social networks, I'd shake him and say, "Don't—"
turns.zh: 所以然后我喜欢说，好吧，我用这个信息做什么？如果我能回到 2003 年的马克，在做 Tribe，最早的三个社交网络之一，我会摇醒他说，“不要——”

turns.en: Your instincts were right there on like multiple multiple levels, like three different industries, right?
turns.zh: 你的直觉在那里是对的，在多个层面，像三个不同的行业，对吧？

turns.en: I mean, Facebook became a pretty big company even though they changed their name eventually.
turns.zh: 我的意思是，Facebook 成为了一家相当大的公司，尽管他们最终改了名字。

turns.en: Um, so yes. And so to be clear, one of the businesses you founded was a precursor to—
turns.zh: 嗯，所以是的。所以澄清一下，你创办的企业之一是——的前身。

turns.en: Yeah. Before Facebook, I started and I started a social network when everything worked. I mean, there wasn't one there. Most social networks back then worked and you'd get an email saying, "Mark wants to be your friend." You'd be like, "Oh, what's that?" Right? And I still managed to fail. That took an act of willpower to fail. I mean, I had to really be determined.
turns.zh: 是的。在 Facebook 之前，我开始了一个社交网络，当一切顺利时。我的意思是，那里没有。当时大多数社交网络都成功了，你会收到一封邮件说，“马克想成为你的朋友。”你会想，“哦，那是什么？”对吧？而我仍然设法失败了。那需要意志力才能失败。我的意思是，我必须非常坚定。

turns.en: And so, so if I could go back and say, Mark, good news for you. That instinct you had, it becomes trillion dollar companies and industries, multiple industries, you're on to something big. Bad news is this one idea ain't gonna hunt.
turns.zh: 所以，所以如果我能回去说，马克，好消息。你有的那个直觉，它变成了万亿美元的公司和行业，多个行业，你发现了大东西。坏消息是这个想法行不通。

turns.en: What do you want to do with that information? What do you want to do with that cheat code? Well, it's a it's a time machine. Right now, I can say, "Oh, thank you, Mark Future, so much. I'm going to just try four or five."
turns.zh: 你想用这个信息做什么？你想用这个作弊码做什么？好吧，那是时间机器。现在，我可以说，“哦，谢谢你，未来的马克，非常感谢。我将尝试四五个。”

turns.en: What's the actional advice to a founder who's getting stuck in this loop?
turns.zh: 对一个陷入这个循环的创始人，有什么可操作的建议？

turns.en: Okay, so that gets to my third piece of advice from the book which is I developed a framework not in time for tribe but I did do it for Zynga that I call proven better new.
turns.zh: 好的，所以这就到了我书中的第三条建议，那就是我开发了一个框架，不是为 Tribe 及时开发的，但我为 Zynga 做了，我称之为“验证、更好、新”。

turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: And this became a religion at Zynga is still a religion for former Zynga people. It became part of the PM culture of Silicon Valley. The idea is whatever I whatever you want to do, you can you can find products similar to yours in the world and you can deconstruct those down to the pixel level of the experience down to in games the mechanic level. In anything though, you can say all of these things make up that experience and I'm going to take what's out there that I know works. It's the most successful. I like it and I'm gonna call that proven and I'm going to be get a PhD in that proven and then I'm going to look at what can I make better. What can I among within that proven?
turns.zh: 这成了 Zynga 的宗教，对前 Zynga 人来说仍然是宗教。它成了硅谷 PM 文化的一部分。想法是无论我——无论你想做什么，你可以在世界上找到类似的产品，你可以解构它们，到体验的像素级别，到游戏中机制级别。在任何事中，你可以说所有这些构成了那个体验，我将采用我知道有效的现有东西。它是最成功的。我喜欢它，我会称之为验证过的，然后我会在那个验证过的上获得博士学位，然后我会看看我能做什么更好。我能在那个验证过的中做什么？

turns.en: Yeah. Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。是的。

turns.en: Or about that product. Can I make something that is again irrefutably better? I mean 10 out of 10 of the existing users say yes.
turns.zh: 或者关于那个产品。我能做出再次无可辩驳地更好的东西吗？我的意思是 10 个现有用户中 10 个都说好。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: If we're allowed to say that at Harvard.
turns.zh: 如果我们在哈佛被允许这么说。

turns.en: With FarmVille, it was the crops and the crop art. Every single person thought it was better, and it was something they really cared about. New is your innovation zone—it's the novel new idea you have—and that idea will fail. One of my mantras, they still say it inside Zynga, is: all new fails. If you assume all new fails, you will almost never be disappointed.
turns.zh: 在 FarmVille 里，就是作物和作物艺术。每个人都觉得它更好，而且他们真的很在意。新东西是你的创新区——你拥有的新颖想法——而那个想法会失败。我的一句口头禅，在 Zynga 内部他们至今还在说：所有新事物都会失败。如果你假设所有新事物都会失败，你几乎永远不会失望。

turns.en: So you create a narrow zone that fails? Meaning if you create a product that hasn't existed, that isn't related to anything else, it will fail.
turns.zh: 所以你创造了一个狭窄的失败区？意思是如果你创造了一个从未存在过的产品，与任何其他东西都无关，它就会失败。

turns.en: All new ideas that are introduced to the world fail at first.
turns.zh: 所有被引入世界的新想法一开始都会失败。

turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: And there's a needle in a haystack—like maybe one in a million. But the point is, okay, if I have too much new in my product, and if you try to make all the proven things new, you're actually going to make them all worse because you don't have the time. And I say it's irresponsible if what you care about is the value in the eyes of your customer, not respect from your peers. You don't have the right to change something that's proven. You have not earned that right. You are not good enough at this and you are not smart enough at this. You're not a PhD in whatever you're building to actually pull this off—to change that many things. To make something that the whole world acknowledges is better, it's usually a teeny teeny thing.
turns.zh: 而且还有大海捞针——可能百万分之一。但重点是，好吧，如果我的产品里有太多新东西，如果你试图把所有经过验证的东西都变成新的，你实际上会让它们都变得更糟，因为你没有时间。我要说，如果你关心的是客户眼中的价值，而不是同行的尊重，那这是不负责任的。你没有权利去改变已经验证过的东西。你还没有赢得那个权利。你在这方面不够好，也不够聪明。你不是你所构建领域的博士，无法真正实现这一点——改变那么多东西。要做出全世界都承认更好的东西，通常是一件非常非常小的事。

turns.en: So what's fascinating about this is the common—you would argue misperception of ideas is literally you're like struck by lightning and you come up with a brilliant new world that no one can see except you. Okay. And that's what you prosecute against. Your argument would be in many ways you're sort of democratizing media generation, right? What you're basically saying is new ideas as you define them are accessible to all.
turns.zh: 所以这有趣的地方在于，常见的——你会说是误解——对想法的看法，字面上就像你被闪电击中，然后想出一个除了你没人能看到的辉煌新世界。好吧。而这就是你所要抨击的。你的论点在很多方面是在民主化媒体生成，对吧？你基本上是在说，你所定义的新想法是所有人都能获得的。

turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: Okay. Which is sort of an interesting point, right? Because most founders, most people would argue that, oh, the idea is the needle in the haystack and you could spend your whole life looking for that idea. I want to have found—if only I had that amazing idea. Your point I believe is everyone can found because the ideas are just right in front of you and what you need to do is go learn that model or that proven—
turns.zh: 好吧。这倒是个有趣的观点，对吧？因为大多数创始人、大多数人会争辩说，哦，想法就是大海捞针，你可能花一辈子寻找那个想法。我想找到——要是我有那个绝妙的想法就好了。我相信你的观点是每个人都能创立，因为想法就在你眼前，你需要做的是去学习那个模型或那个经过验证的——

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: —and try to make it incrementally better.
turns.zh: ——并尝试让它逐步变得更好。

turns.en: Yes. What I would say is at a minimum, whatever it is you're trying to do, if you take this kind of approach, I think you're going to 4x your odds of success. Whether or not that was going to succeed. You have imagined if I had four shots on goal that were all very close to each other and calibrated, probably have four times the chance of succeeding, then one shot on goal, especially if you already—we can already assume your first shot isn't going to work and you're going to learn from each shot. The one thing I'd also add is that is another part of the book is about the importance of road mapping and testing and having a mantra that you want to test more ideas in a week than your industry tests in a year.
turns.zh: 是的。我要说的是，至少，无论你想做什么，如果你采取这种方法，我认为你会把成功几率提高四倍。不管那是否会成功。你可以想象，如果我有四次射门机会，它们彼此非常接近并且经过校准，可能比一次射门机会有四倍的成功机会，尤其是如果你已经——我们可以假设你的第一次射门不会成功，而你会从每次射门中学习。我还要补充的一点是，这也是书中的另一部分，关于路线图和测试的重要性，以及有一个口头禅：你想在一周内测试比你的行业在一年内测试的更多想法。

turns.en: Wow.
turns.zh: 哇。

turns.en: Because if what you build is a testing machine, you build a failure machine, then the rate that you're going to learn is so much faster than everybody else.
turns.zh: 因为如果你构建的是一台测试机器，你就构建了一台失败机器，那么你学习的速度会比其他人快得多。

turns.en: Another one of your controversial points or counterintuitive points is around scale. So tell me how you think—I mean shouldn't every founder be pitching it's all about scale.
turns.zh: 你的另一个有争议或反直觉的观点是关于规模的。所以告诉我你怎么想——我的意思是，难道每个创始人不都应该鼓吹一切在于规模吗？

turns.en: Well, when I was here at HBS, that was the magic word—scale. And this is even long before there was an Amazon, you know, but it was Walmart and the Japanese and being the scalable leader. Yeah, so one of my favorite chapters is about scale. And I hope that no one takes this the wrong way here at HBS, but when I talk to MBAs or when I say you don't need to spend two years getting an MBA, all you need—the fundamental—there's only one point of management, which is how do we get people to do the right thing when we're not in the room. And the first thing is be in the room. Don't delegate. No one's impressed that you're delegating. I say, you know, I don't know why McDonald's has these signs saying over 15 million served. That doesn't make me think my burger is going to be any better. I'm like, I'd rather that the colonel is there making me my burger, you know, like flipping it and really checking the quality. I'm like, I'm not happy that you made 15 million today, right? So the first point is micromanage. And I think now with Elon, things have changed since I started or even wrote the book that now we're starting to kind of fall back in love with the idea of the leaders that are in the details. But it was a bad thing. Micromanagement was a bad thing. So be in the room until you can't possibly be there anymore. Be in every single detail that if you can make a better decision than anybody else, you should.
